subtopic_detail: Antipyretic advice for the well febrile toddler
stem:
A 2 year old boy is brought to your general practice on the second day of a fever. He has a runny nose and a loose cough, and his 4 year old sister had the same illness last week.

He is alert, playing with the toys in your room, drinking well and has had five wet nappies today. Examination of his ears, throat, chest and abdomen is unremarkable and there is no rash.

His mother has been giving paracetamol whenever the thermometer reads above 38 degrees Celsius and asks whether she should also add ibuprofen overnight so that his temperature never climbs high enough to cause a fit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about antipyretic use?

options.text: Alternate paracetamol and ibuprofen four-hourly overnight to hold the temperature below 38 degrees Celsius.
options.rationale: Routine alternating regimens increase dosing errors and are not recommended, and no antipyretic schedule prevents febrile convulsions. It would be reasonable only as a short rescue in a child whose distress is not controlled by a single agent. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) six-hourly only when the fever is making him uncomfortable.
options.rationale: Antipyretics in children are given for comfort, not to normalise a number; the drug is dosed by weight with a stated maximum and titrated to distress rather than to the thermometer. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child
AMH Children's Dosing Companion

options.text: Give ibuprofen 10 mg/kg (maximum 400 mg) six-hourly regularly for five days to prevent a febrile convulsion.
options.rationale: Regular antipyretics do not reduce the risk of a first or recurrent febrile convulsion, so a fixed five day course exposes him to drug risk with no seizure benefit. Ibuprofen would be reasonable as an alternative comfort measure given as required. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Withhold all antipyretics so that the true fever pattern can be documented before his next review.
options.rationale: Fever pattern rarely changes management in a well immunised toddler with a viral illness, and withholding analgesia leaves a distressed child untreated. Withholding is defensible only when a periodic fever syndrome is being formally charted. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg regularly and add tepid sponging every two hours until the temperature settles.
options.rationale: Tepid sponging causes shivering and discomfort without shortening the illness and is no longer advised. Physical cooling belongs to heat stroke management, where the problem is a failure of thermoregulation rather than a raised set point. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Fever is a physiological response to infection rather than a disease in itself, and in a well appearing immunised child over 3 months the priority is finding a source and safety netting rather than lowering the number. Australian paediatric practice treats antipyretics as analgesics: they are given when the child is miserable, and the response to them does not discriminate viral from bacterial illness. Parents commonly believe that untreated fever causes brain injury or seizures, and correcting that belief reduces repeat presentations and medication errors. Height of fever alone is a weak predictor of serious bacterial infection once a child is beyond the young infant age bands. In context, the decision that matters at this visit is not which antipyretic to use but whether a source has been found and what the family should watch for.
key_points: Antipyretics are given for comfort, not to normalise temperature or prevent seizures.
Alternating or combining paracetamol and ibuprofen routinely increases dosing error risk.
Tepid sponging is not recommended for fever from infection.
Response of fever to an antipyretic does not distinguish viral from bacterial illness.
Safety netting advice matters more than the antipyretic choice in a well toddler.
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg per dose to a maximum of 1 g, four to six hourly and no more than four doses in 24 hours, is the Australian paediatric standard; ibuprofen 10 mg/kg per dose to a maximum of 400 mg is the alternative in a well hydrated child.

AMH Children's Dosing Companion

subtopic_detail: Urine testing in the febrile young infant with a positive viral swab
stem:
A 6 week old boy born at 39 weeks is brought to the emergency department with three days of a runny nose and a wet cough. His mother says he now stops part way through feeds to catch his breath and is taking about two thirds of his usual volume.

On examination he has mild subcostal recession with widespread crackles and expiratory wheeze. He has had four wet nappies in the last 12 hours and is alert between coughing bouts.

A nasopharyngeal swab has returned positive for respiratory syncytial virus, and his temperature has been recorded at 38.4 degrees Celsius on two separate occasions in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 58/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius

lead_in: In addition to supportive care, which investigation is most important now?

options.text: Chest radiograph to identify a bacterial focus before any antibiotic is commenced.
options.rationale: Radiographs in bronchiolitis show non-specific changes, drive unnecessary antibiotic prescribing and are not routinely indicated. Imaging would be reasonable if he needed intensive care support or had focal signs with a persistent oxygen requirement. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis

options.text: Venous blood gas and lactate to grade the severity of his respiratory illness.
options.rationale: Blood gases do not guide management in mild to moderate bronchiolitis and severity is graded clinically on feeding, work of breathing and apnoea. A gas is reasonable in the infant with impending respiratory failure. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis

options.text: Full blood count with C-reactive protein to decide whether empirical antibiotics are required.
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers perform poorly as a stand-alone screen in young infants and a normal result does not exclude a urinary tract infection with a positive culture. They belong within a full evaluation, not as a substitute for a urine specimen. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Catheter urine specimen sent for microscopy, culture and antimicrobial sensitivity testing.
options.rationale: Infants under 2 to 3 months with fever carry a meaningful risk of concurrent urinary tract infection even when a respiratory virus is detected, so a sterile specimen is collected rather than assumed unnecessary. A bag specimen is not acceptable because of contamination rates. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis

options.text: Repeat nasopharyngeal testing for pertussis and adenovirus to look for viral co-infection.
options.rationale: Identifying a second virus does not change supportive management and pertussis is unlikely with wheeze, crackles and a documented fever. Pertussis testing would be reasonable with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting and an afebrile course. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis

explanation.summary: A positive viral test lowers but does not abolish the probability of a concurrent bacterial infection, and in the first months of life the bacterial infection that survives that adjustment is almost always in the urinary tract. Australian paediatric practice therefore keeps urine testing in the pathway for a febrile infant under about 3 months even when bronchiolitis is obvious, while dropping routine bloods, imaging and antibiotics. Collection method matters more than the dipstick result: bag specimens have unacceptable contamination rates and a negative dipstick does not exclude infection in this age group. Missed infant urinary tract infection presents later as bacteraemia or as delayed recognition of an underlying tract abnormality. In context, the skill being tested is holding two diagnoses in mind at once rather than letting a confirmed virus close the assessment.
key_points: A detected respiratory virus reduces but does not eliminate serious bacterial infection risk in young infants.
Urinary tract infection is the bacterial infection most often found alongside bronchiolitis.
Catheter or suprapubic specimens are required; bag urine is unreliable.
Routine chest radiographs and blood gases are not indicated in bronchiolitis.
Oxygen saturation target in Australian bronchiolitis guidance is 90%.
explanation.pearls: Concurrent urinary tract infection is found in roughly 1 to 3 in 100 febrile infants under 2 months with bronchiolitis, which is why the urine specimen stays in the pathway after a positive respiratory syncytial virus swab.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Bronchiolitis

RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

subtopic_detail: Parent-recorded fever that has settled before arrival in a young infant
stem:
A 5 week old girl born at term is brought to the emergency department at 2 am. Her parents recorded axillary temperatures of 38.3 and 38.5 degrees Celsius two hours apart at home using a digital thermometer, and they have not given any medicine.

She fed poorly during the evening but has since taken a full 90 mL bottle in the waiting room. She is alert, has a soft fontanelle, no rash, and a normal cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination.

Her temperature in triage is 37.2 degrees Celsius and the resident asks whether the workup can be stood down now that she is afebrile and feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the documented home temperature as fever and proceed with the young infant evaluation.
options.rationale: A reliably measured temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or more at any point counts as fever in an infant under 3 months, and defervescence before arrival does not lower the risk of serious bacterial infection. The evaluation proceeds on the history. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Observe in the short stay unit for six hours and investigate only if the fever returns.
options.rationale: Waiting for the fever to recur delays cultures and antibiotics in the age band with the highest occult bacteraemia risk, and a well interval is common in early infant sepsis. Observation alone suits the well immunised child over 3 months. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Reassure the parents that axillary readings overestimate and arrange a general practice review tomorrow.
options.rationale: Axillary measurement is the recommended route in this age group and a reading of 38 degrees Celsius or more is accepted as fever rather than discounted. Discounting the parental reading is the specific error this presentation tests. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Send a bag urine specimen and discharge her home if the dipstick shows no nitrites at all.
options.rationale: Bag specimens have high contamination rates and nitrites are frequently negative in infants because bladder dwell time is short. A catheter or suprapubic specimen is required if urine is to inform the decision. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection

options.text: Request a full blood count and C-reactive protein and take cultures only if either is abnormal.
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers are insufficiently sensitive to gate culture collection in a young infant and are drawn as part of the evaluation, not as a filter for it. Marker-led triage applies in older children with a clear focus. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Young infants mount unreliable clinical signs, so the assessment pathway is driven by age and by the presence of fever at any point rather than by how the child looks at the moment of triage. Australian emergency practice accepts a reliably measured parental temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or more as fever, because the alternative is to discharge infants whose bacteraemia happened to be between spikes. Reassuring interval features such as a good feed and a settled appearance do not reclassify an infant under 3 months into a low risk group on their own. The consequence of standing the workup down is a missed urinary tract infection, bacteraemia or meningitis that returns hours later in shock. In context, this is a triage decision about whether the child enters the young infant pathway at all, and the threshold for entering it is deliberately low.
key_points: Fever in an infant under 3 months is a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or more, measured at any time.
A reliably measured parent-recorded temperature counts as fever.
Being afebrile and feeding well on arrival does not exclude serious bacterial infection.
Axillary measurement is the recommended route under 3 months.
Inflammatory markers do not have the sensitivity to replace cultures in this age band.
explanation.pearls: Around one in five febrile infants under 3 months with a serious bacterial infection is afebrile at the time of assessment, which is why the history of a measured 38 degrees Celsius is what triggers the pathway.

subtopic_detail: Fever without source in the fully immunised toddler aged 3 to 36 months
stem:
A 14 month old girl is brought to the emergency department with two days of fever reaching 39.6 degrees Celsius. There is no cough, rash, vomiting or loose stools, and her appetite for solids is reduced but she is drinking well.

She is fully immunised for age and has never been unwell before. In the cubicle she is pulling books off the shelf and objects to examination vigorously.

Ears, throat, chest, abdomen and skin are all normal, and after 40 minutes of observation and a careful second look you have still not identified a focus for the fever.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures and commence intravenous ceftriaxone while the culture results are awaited.
options.rationale: Occult bacteraemia is now rare in fully immunised toddlers and empirical parenteral antibiotics in a well child risk masking a urinary tract infection and promoting resistance. This approach belongs to the unwell or unimmunised child. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Arrange a chest radiograph to look for an occult bacterial focus in the lower airway.
options.rationale: Occult pneumonia is unlikely without tachypnoea, hypoxia, cough or focal chest signs, and routine films in this setting mostly generate false positives. Imaging would be reasonable with a persistent oxygen requirement or focal auscultatory findings. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Send a catheter or clean catch urine specimen for microscopy, culture and sensitivities.
options.rationale: Urinary tract infection is the commonest occult bacterial source in a well appearing febrile toddler with no focus, and girls in this age band carry the highest prevalence. A reliable specimen is the single highest yield test. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Urinary tract infection
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily and review him in 48 hours.
options.rationale: Blind oral antibiotics without a source neither treat a urinary pathogen reliably nor cover the diagnosis you have not yet made, and they render a later urine culture uninterpretable. Amoxicillin is reasonable once a susceptible focus such as otitis media is identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Discharge home with antipyretic advice alone and no further investigation on this visit.
options.rationale: Discharging without a urine specimen is the commonest route to a missed febrile urinary tract infection in this age group. Discharge without testing is reasonable once a clear viral source such as an exanthem or bronchiolitis is identified. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Conjugate vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae has collapsed the rate of occult bacteraemia, so the 3 to 36 month fever without source pathway in Australia has narrowed from broad blood testing to targeted urine testing plus structured observation. The well appearing child with normal perfusion and no focus is managed on urine culture and safety netting rather than on the height of the fever. Immunisation status is the main modifier: an incompletely immunised child is reassessed against the pre-vaccine risk profile. Missed urinary tract infection in this age band is the source of most delayed diagnoses and of preventable renal scarring when it recurs. In context, the question is which single investigation changes management in a child who looks well, and in this age band it is almost always the urine.
key_points: Urinary tract infection is the commonest occult source in fever without a focus at 3 to 36 months.
Conjugate vaccines have made occult pneumococcal bacteraemia rare in immunised children.
Height of fever alone is a weak predictor of serious bacterial infection.
Blind oral antibiotics make a subsequent urine culture uninterpretable.
Structured observation and safety netting substitute for broad blood testing in the well child.
explanation.pearls: Prevalence of urinary tract infection approaches 8 in 100 in febrile girls under 2 years with no source, which is why a reliable urine specimen is collected before the child leaves the department.

subtopic_detail: Fever in the asplenic child on penicillin prophylaxis
stem:
A 6 year old boy is brought to a regional emergency department four hours after his mother recorded a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius. He vomited once in the car, has a mild sore throat and is otherwise complaining of nothing.

He is alert and chatty, his peripheries are warm with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, and examination of his chest, abdomen, skin and joints is unremarkable.

He had a splenectomy two years ago for hereditary spherocytosis, has received all the recommended additional vaccines, and his mother confirms she gave his twice daily phenoxymethylpenicillin this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Point of care blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the phenoxymethylpenicillin to four times daily and review him again in 24 hours.
options.rationale: Prophylaxis reduces but does not prevent invasive pneumococcal disease, and breakthrough infection is by definition not controlled by intensifying the same oral agent. Dose adjustment is an outpatient decision, not a response to a febrile episode. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Send a throat swab and blood film and await both results before giving any antibiotic.
options.rationale: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection can progress from well to fatal within hours, so no result is worth waiting for before the first parenteral dose. Swab-led management applies to the child with an intact spleen and a clear pharyngitic focus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and arrange review by his general practitioner the next morning.
options.rationale: Oral therapy with next day review assumes time that an asplenic child may not have, and absorption is unreliable once he starts vomiting. This is reasonable in the immunocompetent child with a defined minor bacterial focus. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Observe him in the department for four hours and discharge if he stays alert and afebrile.
options.rationale: Structured observation is a legitimate strategy in the well immunised child with a spleen, but asplenia removes the reserve that observation relies on. Reassuring appearance at four hours does not exclude early pneumococcal bacteraemia. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Take blood cultures and give intravenous ceftriaxone now, then admit him for observation.
options.rationale: Any fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more in an asplenic child is treated as possible overwhelming post-splenectomy infection with cultures and an immediate broad spectrum parenteral dose, regardless of how well he looks. Ceftriaxone covers the encapsulated organisms that prophylaxis and vaccination can miss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Asplenia and hyposplenism remove the main site of clearance for opsonised encapsulated bacteria, so Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis can produce fulminant bacteraemia with little warning. Australian practice pairs lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis and an expanded vaccine schedule with an emergency rule: any fever means immediate parenteral antibiotics after cultures, not a period of watching. Families are issued with a standby antibiotic and a written action plan precisely because the window between first fever and shock can be measured in hours. Case fatality in overwhelming post-splenectomy infection remains high even in well resourced centres, and almost all of the preventable deaths involve a delayed first dose. In context, the reasoning tested here is that host factors, not the child's appearance, set the threshold for treatment.
key_points: Fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more in an asplenic child mandates immediate parenteral antibiotics after cultures.
Prophylactic penicillin and vaccination reduce but do not eliminate invasive disease.
Streptococcus pneumoniae causes the majority of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
Appearance at presentation does not predict the speed of deterioration.
Families should hold a standby antibiotic and a written action plan.
explanation.pearls: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection carries a case fatality of up to 50% and most commonly involves Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is why ceftriaxone is given within the first hour of any fever rather than after results return.

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of fever in the child returned from a malarious region
stem:
A 9 year old girl presents with three days of fever reaching 39.2 degrees Celsius, associated with shaking chills, headache and two episodes of vomiting. She returned ten days ago from three weeks visiting family in eastern Indonesia.

She has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash. Her abdomen is soft with a spleen tip palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin, and the rest of the examination is normal.

Her mother says the atovaquone with proguanil tablets were started late and several doses were missed during the trip.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), white cell count 4.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (2-20)

lead_in: Which investigation is most important now?

options.text: Blood culture with abdominal ultrasound looking for a hepatic or splenic collection.
options.rationale: A collection would be expected to produce localised pain, tenderness or a swinging fever over a longer course, and imaging does not address the time critical diagnosis. Ultrasound is reasonable once films are negative and fever persists beyond a week. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Thick and thin blood films with a rapid diagnostic test, repeated 12 to 24 hourly.
options.rationale: Fever in a child returned from a malarious area is malaria until excluded, and a single negative film does not exclude it, so three sets are collected over 48 hours alongside an antigen test. Thrombocytopenia with anaemia and splenomegaly strengthens the indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Dengue NS1 antigen with paired serology sent to the state reference laboratory.
options.rationale: Dengue is a genuine differential in this itinerary but testing it first delays a diagnosis that can kill within 24 hours, and rigors with splenomegaly favour the parasitaemic illness. Dengue testing is sent in parallel, not instead. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines

options.text: Enteric fever serology with stool culture and a full blood count taken today.
options.rationale: Serology for enteric fever is insensitive and non-specific and is not used for diagnosis in Australia, where blood culture is the test of choice. Stool culture yields late in the illness and does not exclude a parasitaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Epstein-Barr virus serology with liver function tests and a repeat full blood count.
options.rationale: Infectious mononucleosis can produce fever, splenomegaly and cytopenias, but it does not cause rigors and it does not require exclusion within hours. This becomes reasonable after malaria has been excluded on serial films. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: Imported malaria remains the single most time critical diagnosis in a febrile returned traveller, because Plasmodium falciparum can progress from uncomplicated fever to cerebral involvement or shock within a day. Chemoprophylaxis that was partial, late or poorly adhered to offers essentially no protection and must never be used to lower suspicion. Microscopy of thick and thin films gives both species and parasite density, which determine whether the child needs parenteral therapy, and rapid antigen tests supplement but do not replace it. The classical periodic fever pattern is usually absent in the first presentation, so waiting for it delays diagnosis. In context, the reasoning step is that a plausible alternative diagnosis does not excuse skipping the one that is lethal fastest.
key_points: Fever in a returned traveller from a malarious area is malaria until excluded.
Three sets of thick and thin films over 48 hours are needed before malaria is excluded.
Incomplete or late chemoprophylaxis does not reduce the pre-test probability meaningfully.
Parasite density from microscopy determines parenteral versus oral therapy.
Thrombocytopenia with anaemia and splenomegaly is a common early laboratory pattern.
explanation.pearls: Plasmodium falciparum from South East Asia and Oceania almost always presents within 3 months of return, and 90% of cases declare themselves within 1 month, so a recent itinerary is the highest yield question in the history.

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for prolonged fever after travel to South Asia
stem:
An 11 year old boy has had seven days of fever that has climbed a little higher each evening, now reaching 39.4 degrees Celsius. He has a dull headache, abdominal discomfort and was constipated for four days before passing loose stools yesterday.

He returned eight days ago from six weeks staying with relatives in rural Uttar Pradesh. Three sets of thick and thin films have been negative and a rapid antigen test for malaria is negative.

His abdomen is mildly distended with a spleen tip palpable, and his pulse is 88 per minute while his temperature is 39.4 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 3.4 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (5-40), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg (maximum 750 mg) twice daily for seven days from today.
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolone resistance in Salmonella Typhi acquired in South Asia now exceeds 90%, so ciprofloxacin fails in exactly the geography this itinerary describes. It remains reasonable for a susceptible isolate acquired elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) three times daily for fourteen days from today.
options.rationale: Amoxicillin has no reliable activity against contemporary multidrug resistant enteric fever isolates and does not treat the intracellular phase adequately. It would only be appropriate for a fully susceptible isolate as step down therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral metronidazole 10 mg/kg (maximum 400 mg) three times daily for seven days from today.
options.rationale: Metronidazole targets anaerobes and invasive amoebiasis, which would present with dysentery or a tender liver rather than a stepwise fever with relative bradycardia. It has no role against Salmonella Typhi. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) once daily for fourteen days from today.
options.rationale: A third generation cephalosporin is the Australian empirical choice for suspected enteric fever acquired in South Asia because it remains active against multidrug and extensively drug resistant strains. Parenteral therapy is used while he is unwell, with duration guided by response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) once daily for three days only from today.
options.rationale: Azithromycin is an appropriate agent for uncomplicated enteric fever but requires about seven days, so a three day course is a relapse regimen rather than a cure. The distinction from the correct option is route and duration, not spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Enteric fever is the second diagnosis to work through once malaria has been excluded in a child returned from South Asia, and its signature is a fever that rises stepwise over a week with relative bradycardia, leucopenia and mildly deranged transaminases. Blood culture is the diagnostic test; serology is not used in Australia because of poor performance. Resistance patterns are geographically determined, and extensively drug resistant Salmonella Typhi from Pakistan and neighbouring regions has removed fluoroquinolones and older agents from empirical use. Untreated, the illness progresses over weeks to intestinal perforation and haemorrhage in the third week. In context, the reasoning being tested is that the travel itinerary chooses the antibiotic, not just the diagnosis.
key_points: Blood culture is the diagnostic test for enteric fever; serology has no role in Australia.
Stepwise fever with relative bradycardia and leucopenia is the typical pattern.
Fluoroquinolone resistance is near universal in South Asian isolates.
Ceftriaxone is the Australian empirical choice pending susceptibilities.
Untreated disease risks intestinal perforation in the third week.
explanation.pearls: Relative bradycardia, where the pulse fails to rise by about 10 beats per minute for each degree Celsius above 38, is a classic but only moderately sensitive sign of enteric fever and should never be used to exclude it.

subtopic_detail: Blood culture sampling in the febrile child with a central venous access device
stem:
A 7 year old girl on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is brought in by her father after a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius at home, now 38.9 degrees Celsius in the department.

She is alert and talking, her peripheries are warm with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, and there is no cough, dysuria, rash or abdominal tenderness. The exit site of her double lumen tunnelled central line is clean and non-tender.

Her full blood count taken on arrival shows a neutrophil count of 3.2 x10^9/L, and the nurse is drawing up the first antibiotic dose while you decide how blood should be collected.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-155), white cell count 5.6 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), neutrophils 3.2 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to blood culture collection?

options.text: A single set drawn from the lumen most recently used to deliver her chemotherapy.
options.rationale: Sampling one lumen misses infection confined to the other, which is common in double lumen devices colonised at different times. Single lumen sampling is acceptable only when a device has one lumen. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia

options.text: A single peripheral set only, since the exit site shows no redness, discharge or tenderness.
options.rationale: A clean exit site does not exclude intraluminal biofilm infection, which is the usual mechanism in tunnelled lines. Peripheral only sampling also forfeits the differential time to positivity that identifies a line source. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia

options.text: Cultures deferred until her temperature again exceeds 39 degrees Celsius on repeat measurement.
options.rationale: Deferring cultures delays the first antibiotic dose, and a documented 38 degrees Celsius or more in a child on chemotherapy is already the trigger regardless of the neutrophil count. Waiting for a higher spike has no evidence base. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia

options.text: One set from a single lumen plus surface swabs from the exit site and nares.
options.rationale: Surface swabs identify colonisation rather than bloodstream infection and cannot guide treatment of a device infection. Nasal swabs belong to decolonisation programs, not to the febrile assessment. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia

options.text: Paired sets from a peripheral vein and from each lumen of her central venous line.
options.rationale: Sampling every lumen plus a peripheral vein maximises yield and allows differential time to positivity to identify the line as the source, which determines whether the device must be removed. Antibiotics follow immediately and are not delayed for collection. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile neutropenia
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: A child receiving chemotherapy who develops fever is treated as having a possible bloodstream infection irrespective of the neutrophil count, because mucosal barrier injury and an indwelling device are independent portals of entry. The central venous access device is both the likeliest source and the reason infection can be occult, since biofilm within a lumen produces no external signs. Paired sampling from every lumen and from a peripheral vein is what allows differential time to positivity, the test that distinguishes a line infection from a secondary bacteraemia and therefore decides whether the line comes out. Sampling must never delay the first antibiotic dose, which is targeted within an hour of arrival. In context, the reasoning is about preserving a diagnostic decision that will be made 24 hours later, without losing any minutes now.
key_points: Fever in a child on chemotherapy triggers cultures and antibiotics regardless of neutrophil count.
Every lumen of a multi-lumen device is sampled, plus a peripheral vein.
Differential time to positivity of 2 hours or more suggests the line is the source.
A clean exit site does not exclude intraluminal infection.
Collection must not delay the first antibiotic dose beyond one hour.
explanation.pearls: A central line culture flagging positive at least 2 hours before a simultaneously drawn peripheral culture indicates a line associated bloodstream infection, and Staphylococcus aureus, Candida or Pseudomonas in that setting mandates device removal.

subtopic_detail: Stopping empirical antibiotics after a viral cerebrospinal fluid result in an infant
stem:
A 6 week old boy was admitted two days ago with a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius and marked irritability. A full evaluation including lumbar puncture was performed on arrival and he was started on intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin.

He has now been afebrile for 18 hours, is taking full feeds, settles easily in his mother's arms and has a soft fontanelle with a normal neurological examination.

The laboratory has telephoned to report that blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures remain sterile at 36 hours and that the cerebrospinal fluid enterovirus polymerase chain reaction is positive.

data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 46 x10^6/L (0-5) with 90% lymphocytes, red cells 4 x10^6/L, protein 0.55 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.2 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 5.0 mmol/L, Gram stain no organisms seen
data_table.Blood: White cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intravenous cefotaxime to complete a seven day course and then reassess him.
options.rationale: A seven day parenteral course treats proven bacterial meningitis, which sterile cultures and a positive viral result at 36 hours make unlikely. Continuing exposes him to line complications and prolonged admission without benefit. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin for five days and discharge him with community nurse review.
options.rationale: Oral step down is not a recognised pathway for suspected meningitis and would treat an infection that has been excluded rather than one that has been proven. Step down oral therapy applies to culture proven urinary tract infection. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.text: Cease antibiotics and discharge him with general practice review within the next 24 hours.
options.rationale: Sterile cultures at 36 hours with a positive enterovirus result, a lymphocytic profile, a normal cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glucose ratio and clinical recovery permit antibiotics to stop and discharge with early review. Enteroviral meningitis in a well infant needs no specific therapy. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.text: Add intravenous aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture within the next 24 hours for review.
options.rationale: Aciclovir covers herpes simplex, which is suggested by seizures, focal signs, transaminitis or vesicles rather than by a well feeding afebrile infant with a positive enterovirus result. Repeat sampling is reserved for gram negative or unresponsive proven bacterial disease. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.text: Continue antibiotics until cultures have remained sterile for a full 72 hours before stopping.
options.rationale: Modern automated culture systems flag the great majority of true positives by 36 to 48 hours, so a further day and a half adds cost and cannulation without changing the answer. A 72 hour rule is reasonable in a partially treated infant whose cultures were taken after antibiotics. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

explanation.summary: Enteroviruses are the commonest cause of aseptic meningitis in infancy and typically produce a modest lymphocytic pleocytosis with a normal cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glucose ratio and a mildly raised protein. Polymerase chain reaction on cerebrospinal fluid shortens admissions and antibiotic courses substantially, which is its main clinical value. The decision to stop antibiotics rests on the combination of a positive viral result, sterile cultures at 36 to 48 hours and a child who is clinically well, not on any one of those alone. Neonates in the first two weeks of life are the exception, since enteroviral sepsis syndrome with hepatitis and myocarditis can be severe and warrants continued inpatient care. In context, the reasoning being tested is when accumulated negative evidence is strong enough to actively stop treatment rather than to continue by default.
key_points: Enterovirus is the commonest cause of aseptic meningitis in infants.
A cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glucose ratio above 0.6 argues against bacterial meningitis.
Automated blood culture systems flag most true positives within 36 to 48 hours.
Antibiotics stop on the combination of viral detection, sterile cultures and clinical recovery.
Neonatal enteroviral sepsis with hepatitis or myocarditis is the important exception.
explanation.pearls: A cerebrospinal fluid to plasma glucose ratio below 0.4 is the single most useful laboratory pointer to bacterial meningitis in a child, and it is preserved in enteroviral disease.

subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia detected during paediatric septic shock resuscitation
stem:
A 3 year old boy weighing 15 kg is brought in by ambulance with two days of fever and a day of refusing all fluids. He is difficult to rouse, his knees and hands are mottled and his capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally.

Intraosseous access has been secured in the proximal tibia, blood cultures have been drawn, intravenous ceftriaxone has been given and a 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride has run over eight minutes.

His conscious state has not improved after the bolus and the bedside glucose meter reads 2.0 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 182/min, blood pressure 82/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 96% on 8 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 2.0 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose intravenously and recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia in a shocked child is corrected immediately with 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose, which delivers about 200 mg/kg, and the level is rechecked within 15 minutes. Failure to correct it prolongs the depressed conscious state and worsens the lactate. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Start a maintenance infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose and recheck hourly.
options.rationale: A maintenance infusion delivers glucose far too slowly to reverse a level of 2.0 mmol/L in a child who is already obtunded. It is the correct measure after the bolus has restored the level, to prevent rebound. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Give 5 mL/kg of 10% glucose intravenously and recheck the blood glucose in 30 minutes.
options.rationale: This overshoots the recommended bolus volume, risking a hyperosmolar swing and rebound hypoglycaemia, and a 30 minute recheck is too slow in a shocked child. The volume rather than the concentration is the error here. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Give intramuscular glucagon 0.5 mg and recheck the blood glucose again in 15 minutes.
options.rationale: Glucagon depends on hepatic glycogen stores that are depleted after two days of poor intake and works poorly in sepsis, and it is reserved for hypoglycaemia without vascular access. Access is already established here. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Give a further 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 10 minutes and reassess him.
options.rationale: A second fluid bolus is indeed required in fluid responsive shock, but it does nothing for a glucose of 2.0 mmol/L and leaves a treatable cause of his conscious state uncorrected. Glucose is given first and the bolus follows. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: Hypoglycaemia is common in young children with sepsis because hepatic glycogen stores are small, intake has usually stopped and metabolic demand is high, and it is one of the few immediately reversible contributors to a depressed conscious state. Australian paediatric sepsis pathways build a bedside glucose into the first set of observations for exactly this reason, alongside lactate and blood cultures. The correction is a weight based bolus of 10% glucose followed by a glucose containing infusion, because a bolus alone commonly rebounds within the hour. A true blood sample for insulin, cortisol, growth hormone and ketones should be saved before correction when the cause is unexplained, but resuscitation is never delayed to obtain it. In context, the reasoning being tested is recognising a second, separate problem inside a resuscitation that is otherwise running correctly.
key_points: Bedside glucose is part of the first observation set in paediatric sepsis.
Correct symptomatic hypoglycaemia with 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose intravenously or intraosseously.
Follow the bolus with a glucose containing infusion to prevent rebound.
Glucagon is a rescue for hypoglycaemia without vascular access and fails with depleted glycogen.
Recheck the glucose within 15 minutes of the bolus.
explanation.pearls: A 2 mL/kg bolus of 10% glucose delivers 200 mg/kg and typically raises the blood glucose by 3 to 4 mmol/L, which is why the recheck happens at 15 minutes rather than at the next hourly observation.

subtopic_detail: Escalation to intraosseous access when cannulation fails in a shocked infant
stem:
A 4 month old girl weighing 6 kg is brought to a district emergency department with 12 hours of fever and reduced feeding. She is mottled to the elbows and knees, her capillary refill is 5 seconds and she responds only to painful stimulus.

The sepsis pathway has been activated, oxygen is running and the drugs are drawn up. Her temperature is 38.8 degrees Celsius and her blood pressure is 62/34 mmHg.

Three attempts at peripheral cannulation by two clinicians over the past two minutes have all failed and no further visible or palpable veins remain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 198/min, blood pressure 62/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 94% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to deliver resuscitation?

options.text: Persist with further peripheral attempts while giving intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg now.
options.rationale: An intramuscular dose is a pre-hospital compromise when no other route exists, and absorption is unreliable in a shocked, vasoconstricted infant. Continuing to hunt for veins also delays fluid, which she needs as much as the antibiotic. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access

options.text: Insert an intraosseous needle and give the fluid bolus and first antibiotic through it.
options.rationale: After two failed attempts or 90 seconds in a shocked child, intraosseous access is the recommended route and takes every resuscitation drug and fluid at standard doses. It is faster and has a higher first pass success rate than any alternative in this situation. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access
Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Request an ultrasound guided femoral central line from the retrieval intensive care team.
options.rationale: Central venous cannulation in an infant takes far longer, needs an operator with specific paediatric experience and is not a first line access strategy in shock. It is appropriate once resuscitation is under way through another route. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access

options.text: Pass a nasogastric tube and give oral rehydration solution while vascular access is sought.
options.rationale: Enteral fluid cannot reverse decompensated shock because splanchnic perfusion is already diverted, and it risks aspiration in an infant with a depressed conscious state. Nasogastric rehydration is a gastroenteritis strategy in a child who is not shocked. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Perform a venous cutdown on the long saphenous vein at the ankle under anaesthetic.
options.rationale: Cutdown has been superseded by intraosseous devices, which are quicker and need less training, and it wastes minutes that determine outcome. It survives only as a rescue when intraosseous insertion has failed at both available sites. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Intraosseous access

explanation.summary: Time to first antibiotic and time to first fluid bolus are the two process measures most strongly associated with survival in paediatric sepsis, and both depend entirely on vascular access. Australian paediatric emergency practice therefore sets an explicit ceiling on cannulation attempts in a shocked child before moving to the intraosseous route, rather than leaving it to individual judgement. Any drug, fluid or blood product that can be given intravenously can be given intraosseously at the same dose, and blood drawn on insertion is acceptable for culture, glucose, gas and cross match. The proximal tibia is preferred in infants because the landmark is reliable and the growth plate is easily avoided, with the distal femur as the alternative. In context, the reasoning being tested is knowing when to abandon a familiar technique that is failing rather than persisting with it.
key_points: Move to intraosseous access after two failed attempts or 90 seconds in a shocked child.
All resuscitation drugs and fluids may be given intraosseously at intravenous doses.
Blood drawn on insertion is suitable for culture, glucose, gas and cross match.
Proximal tibia is the preferred site in infants, distal femur the alternative.
Intramuscular antibiotic is a pre-hospital compromise, not a substitute for access.
explanation.pearls: Intraosseous insertion has a first attempt success rate above 80% in children and takes under a minute, compared with a median of several minutes and repeated failures for peripheral cannulation in decompensated shock.

subtopic_detail: Induction agent selection for intubation in paediatric septic shock
stem:
A 5 year old girl weighing 18 kg has received 40 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid and is on a peripheral adrenaline infusion for septic shock. Blood cultures were taken and ceftriaxone was given within 30 minutes of arrival.

Her work of breathing has increased over the last 20 minutes, she is now grunting, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score has fallen from 13 to 9. The retrieval team is 90 minutes away and the consultant has decided to intubate her here.

Her blood pressure is 72/38 mmHg and her venous lactate has risen from 3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 72/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 92% on 15 L/min via reservoir mask, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), pH 7.21, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which induction agent is most appropriate?

options.text: Propofol 2 mg/kg intravenously with fentanyl 1 microgram/kg as the induction sequence.
options.rationale: Propofol causes dose dependent vasodilation and myocardial depression and can precipitate cardiac arrest in a child who is already vasoplegic and catecholamine dependent. It is a reasonable choice in a haemodynamically stable child. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction

options.text: Thiopentone 4 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
options.rationale: Thiopentone is a potent venodilator and negative inotrope, so it shares propofol's haemodynamic problem without offering any advantage here. Its niche is control of raised intracranial pressure in a normotensive patient. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction

options.text: Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg intravenously with suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
options.rationale: Midazolam gives unreliable depth at haemodynamically tolerable doses and still lowers systemic vascular resistance, and suxamethonium risks hyperkalaemia in a hypoperfused acidotic child. It is a sedation agent rather than an induction agent. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction

options.text: Ketamine 1 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
options.rationale: Ketamine preserves sympathetic tone and systemic vascular resistance, making it the agent of choice for induction in shock, and rocuronium avoids the hyperkalaemia risk of a depolarising blocker. The dose is reduced from standard because circulating catecholamines are already high. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
options.rationale: Etomidate preserves blood pressure as well as ketamine does, but a single dose inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase and suppresses the cortisol response for hours in a child whose adrenal reserve is already stressed. That is the distinction between the two haemodynamically stable agents, and it keeps etomidate out of septic shock. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Rapid sequence induction

explanation.summary: Intubation is one of the highest risk moments in paediatric septic shock, because induction removes the sympathetic drive that has been maintaining blood pressure and positive pressure ventilation reduces venous return at the same instant. The Australian approach is to optimise before inducing: fluid loaded, vasoactive infusion already running, push dose vasopressor and fluid drawn up, and an agent chosen for cardiovascular stability. Ketamine is preferred because it maintains systemic vascular resistance through indirect sympathomimetic action, although its direct myocardial depressant effect appears when endogenous catecholamines are exhausted, which is why the dose is reduced. Rocuronium is favoured over suxamethonium in the acidotic, hypoperfused child. In context, the reasoning being tested is anticipating a predictable physiological insult rather than reacting to it after the tube is in.
key_points: Induction in shock removes compensatory sympathetic tone and can precipitate arrest.
Ketamine preserves systemic vascular resistance and is the preferred agent in shock.
Reduce the induction dose when endogenous catecholamine drive is already maximal.
Rocuronium is preferred to suxamethonium in acidosis and hypoperfusion.
Fluid, vasoactive infusion and push dose vasopressor should be ready before induction.
explanation.pearls: Ketamine at 1 mg/kg rather than the usual 2 mg/kg is the shock dose, because its indirect sympathomimetic effect fails in catecholamine depleted patients and its direct negative inotropy is then unmasked.

subtopic_detail: Ward recognition of deterioration in a febrile child already under observation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident asked to review a 2 year old boy on the ward. He was admitted eight hours ago with fever and reduced oral intake and has been having hourly observations.

Two hours ago he was given paracetamol and took 10 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution without vomiting. His temperature has now settled to 37.8 degrees Celsius but his heart rate has not come down with it.

He was chatting to his mother at the last review and now has to be repeatedly roused for observations, with cool knees and a central capillary refill of 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Difficult to rouse, cool peripheries to the knees, central capillary refill 4 seconds, no rash, moist mucous membranes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate on the sepsis pathway with cultures, lactate and intravenous antibiotics now.
options.rationale: Altered conscious state with persistent tachycardia after antipyretic and delayed central capillary refill are pathway triggers, and the bundle of cultures, lactate, antibiotics and fluid follows immediately. Fever settling does not reduce the risk. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway
RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Repeat the paracetamol dose now and reassess his heart rate again in a further hour.
options.rationale: He is no longer significantly febrile, so a further antipyretic treats nothing and buys an hour that the perfusion findings say he does not have. Repeat antipyretic is reasonable when tachycardia tracks a high temperature in an otherwise well child. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Arrange an urgent chest radiograph to identify the source before any antibiotic is given.
options.rationale: Source identification is valuable but must not precede the first antibiotic dose, and transferring a shocked toddler to the radiology department is itself a risk. Imaging follows resuscitation once he is stable. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Give a further 10 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution and continue hourly observations.
options.rationale: Oral fluid cannot resuscitate a child with cool peripheries and a 4 second capillary refill, and a drowsy toddler is at risk of aspiration. Enteral rehydration remains appropriate for mild to moderate dehydration without shock. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Request an urgent full blood count and C-reactive protein before starting any treatment.
options.rationale: Inflammatory markers are neither sensitive nor timely enough to gate antibiotics in suspected septic shock and will not be back within the hour that matters. They are drawn with the cultures, not instead of treatment. (Source: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: Australian paediatric sepsis pathways were built around ward and emergency recognition failures rather than around treatment failures, because the interventions are simple once the child is recognised. The triggers that matter most are altered behaviour reported by a parent or nurse, tachycardia that persists after fever and pain are treated, and abnormal peripheral perfusion, since blood pressure is preserved until very late in children. A falling temperature is not reassurance; late sepsis in young children can present with normal or low temperature. The bundle that follows is deliberately fixed in order: access, cultures, antibiotic within the hour, then fluid in 10 to 20 mL/kg aliquots with reassessment after each. In context, the reasoning being tested is reading a trend across observations rather than a single set of numbers.
key_points: Persistent tachycardia after antipyretic and fluid is a sepsis pathway trigger.
Altered conscious state and delayed central capillary refill outweigh a normal blood pressure.
Hypotension is a late and pre-terminal finding in paediatric shock.
Antibiotics are given within one hour and are not delayed for imaging or markers.
A settling temperature does not reduce the probability of sepsis.
explanation.pearls: Parental or nursing report that the child is not behaving normally is an independent trigger in Australian paediatric sepsis pathways and outperforms any single vital sign at the recognition stage.

subtopic_detail: Vasoactive selection in vasodilated fluid refractory septic shock
stem:
An 8 year old girl weighing 26 kg has had three days of fever and is now hypotensive. Blood cultures were taken, ceftriaxone was given within 25 minutes and she has received 60 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid in 20 mL/kg aliquots over 40 minutes.

Her chest remains clear, her liver edge is not palpable and there is no gallop rhythm. She is drowsy but rousable and her urine output over the last hour was 0.3 mL/kg/hour.

Her hands and feet are warm to the touch with bounding pulses and a capillary refill under 1 second, and her blood pressure remains 78/30 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, blood pressure 78/30 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L, base excess -7 mmol/L

lead_in: Which vasoactive agent is most appropriate now?

options.text: Adrenaline infusion started at 0.05 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the agent for cold shock with poor contractility and vasoconstriction, and its beta 2 effect can lower systemic vascular resistance further in a vasodilated child. The distinction from the correct option is which adrenergic receptor the physiology calls for. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Dobutamine infusion started at 5 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
options.rationale: Dobutamine is an inodilator that would worsen an already low systemic vascular resistance and widen the pulse pressure further. It suits low cardiac output states with adequate filling and high resistance. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
options.rationale: Warm peripheries, bounding pulses, flash capillary refill and a wide pulse pressure after adequate fluid describe vasodilated shock, where an alpha predominant vasoconstrictor restores perfusion pressure. Peripheral administration is acceptable short term while central access and retrieval are arranged. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis
Clinical Excellence Commission: Paediatric Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Milrinone infusion started at 0.25 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
options.rationale: Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that vasodilates and has a long half life, so it is difficult to reverse if the blood pressure falls further. Its place is in low output states after myocardial dysfunction is demonstrated. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

options.text: Vasopressin infusion started at 0.0003 units/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
options.rationale: Vasopressin is a second or third line adjunct in catecholamine resistant shock and is not started before a conventional vasopressor. It also carries a real risk of peripheral and splanchnic ischaemia. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Sepsis

explanation.summary: Paediatric septic shock is classified at the bedside into cold and warm phenotypes, and the distinction drives the vasoactive choice because the underlying haemodynamic defect differs. Cold shock, which is commoner in young children and in hospital acquired sepsis, shows narrow pulse pressure, cool mottled peripheries and prolonged capillary refill, and responds to adrenaline. Warm shock, commoner in older children and adolescents with community acquired sepsis, shows bounding pulses, flash refill, warm extremities and a wide pulse pressure, and responds to noradrenaline. Both are started only after adequate volume resuscitation, and both can be run through a large peripheral or intraosseous line for a short period while central access is obtained. In context, the reasoning being tested is matching a drug to a measured physiology rather than reaching for the drug the pathway names most often.
key_points: Warm shock shows bounding pulses, flash capillary refill and a wide pulse pressure.
Noradrenaline is the vasoactive of choice in warm vasodilated septic shock.
Adrenaline is the agent for cold shock with poor contractility and vasoconstriction.
Vasoactives are started after fluid resuscitation, not before it.
Peripheral or intraosseous infusion is acceptable short term with close site monitoring.
explanation.pearls: A diastolic pressure below about half the systolic in a shocked child indicates a low systemic vascular resistance state and points to noradrenaline rather than adrenaline.

subtopic_detail: Carriage clearance for the index case after treated invasive meningococcal disease
stem:
A 14 year old boy is on day five of intravenous benzylpenicillin for invasive meningococcal disease confirmed by blood polymerase chain reaction. He has been afebrile for 48 hours, his rash has faded and he is eating normally.

The public health unit has already contacted his household and all four members have taken their clearance antibiotics. His school has been notified and no further cases have occurred.

He is ready for discharge this afternoon and his mother asks whether he himself needs to take anything before going home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action before he is discharged?

options.text: No further antibiotic is required because he has completed a full treatment course.
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin treats invasive disease but does not reliably eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage, so the index case can reinfect contacts after discharge. This answer would be correct had he been treated with ceftriaxone. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines

options.text: Give rifampicin 10 mg/kg once daily for five days before he leaves the ward today.
options.rationale: Rifampicin is an accepted clearance agent but the regimen is twice daily for two days, so a once daily five day course is neither the treatment nor the clearance schedule. The near miss here is dose interval and duration, not drug choice. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines

options.text: Repeat a nasopharyngeal swab and treat only if meningococci are subsequently grown.
options.rationale: Culture of nasopharyngeal carriage is insensitive and slow, and clearance is given empirically rather than swab directed. Swabbing delays discharge and risks false reassurance. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines

options.text: Give a further 48 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin before discharge is considered.
options.rationale: Extending treatment adds days of admission without addressing carriage, since the issue is the drug's poor nasopharyngeal penetration rather than an inadequate duration. Five to seven days is a complete course for meningococcal disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose before he leaves the ward today.
options.rationale: A patient treated with benzylpenicillin needs a carriage clearance dose before discharge, and a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin is the preferred Australian regimen in this age group. Ceftriaxone treated patients need no clearance dose. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines)
source_refs: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Series of National Guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Control of invasive meningococcal disease depends on interrupting nasopharyngeal carriage as well as treating the infected patient, because most transmission comes from asymptomatic carriers and from an inadequately cleared index case. Third generation cephalosporins reach the nasopharynx well enough that a treatment course also clears carriage, but benzylpenicillin and chloramphenicol do not, so a clearance dose is added before discharge. Household and intimate contacts are identified and treated by the public health unit, and notification occurs on clinical suspicion rather than on laboratory confirmation. Vaccination of contacts may be recommended in addition to chemoprophylaxis depending on the serogroup identified. In context, the reasoning being tested is that treating the patient and protecting the community are separate tasks with separate drug requirements.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin does not reliably clear nasopharyngeal meningococcal carriage.
Ceftriaxone treated index cases require no additional clearance antibiotic.
Single dose ciprofloxacin is the preferred Australian clearance regimen in adolescents.
Rifampicin clearance is twice daily for two days when ciprofloxacin is unsuitable.
Notification to the public health unit is made on clinical suspicion, not on confirmation.
explanation.pearls: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg as a single oral dose clears meningococcal carriage in over 90% of people within 24 hours, and unlike rifampicin it does not interact with the combined oral contraceptive pill.

subtopic_detail: Fever without source in the incompletely immunised toddler
stem:
A 15 month old boy presents with 36 hours of fever peaking at 39.9 degrees Celsius. He is miserable when the fever climbs but settles, smiles and accepts a bottle after paracetamol.

Examination of his ears, throat, chest, abdomen, skin and joints is normal, his neck is supple and his fontanelle has closed. He has had four wet nappies today and his capillary refill is 2 seconds.

His parents have declined all childhood vaccinations, so he has never received a conjugate pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.6 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with antipyretic advice and general practitioner review in 48 hours if unwell.
options.rationale: Discharge without investigation relies on the herd and individual protection that conjugate vaccines provide, which this child does not have. It is the correct approach in the fully immunised, well appearing child of the same age. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture now because he has never been immunised against Haemophilus.
options.rationale: Lumbar puncture is driven by clinical features of meningitis or a toxic appearance, neither of which he has with a supple neck and a normal conscious state. Immunisation status raises the bacteraemia risk but does not by itself indicate cerebrospinal fluid sampling. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Meningitis and encephalitis

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg now and arrange review in the department tomorrow.
options.rationale: Blind parenteral antibiotics before cultures are taken compromise every subsequent culture and treat a bacteraemia that has not been demonstrated. Ceftriaxone first is appropriate for the toxic appearing child, where treatment cannot wait. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

options.text: Take blood culture and catheter urine, then reassess in the department after four hours.
options.rationale: An incompletely immunised child sits in the pre-vaccine risk profile for occult pneumococcal and Haemophilus bacteraemia, so cultures plus a urine specimen and a period of structured observation are indicated before any disposition decision. Antibiotics are withheld pending the cultures unless he deteriorates. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child
Australian Immunisation Handbook

options.text: Perform a chest radiograph and start oral amoxicillin if any consolidation is demonstrated.
options.rationale: Occult pneumonia is unlikely without tachypnoea, hypoxia or focal signs, and a film alone does not address the urinary tract or the bloodstream. Imaging becomes reasonable if the fever persists with a respiratory component. (Source: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child)
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Febrile child

explanation.summary: The Australian fever without source pathway for children aged 3 to 36 months was rewritten around conjugate vaccination, which reduced occult pneumococcal bacteraemia from roughly 3 to 5 in 100 to well under 1 in 100 in immunised children. A child who has received no conjugate doses does not inherit that reduction, so the assessment reverts to blood culture, urine culture and a period of observation rather than urine testing alone. The observation period matters because the appearance of a bacteraemic toddler often changes over hours, and the reassessment is what converts an outpatient plan into an inpatient one. Empirical antibiotics are still not automatic in the well appearing child, since they blunt culture yield and drive resistance without changing the outcome of a self limiting viral illness. In context, the reasoning being tested is adjusting a population level pathway to an individual whose risk profile sits outside the population it was built for.
key_points: Conjugate vaccination is the main determinant of occult bacteraemia risk at 3 to 36 months.
Unimmunised children are assessed against the pre-vaccine risk profile.
Blood culture plus urine culture and structured observation replace urine testing alone.
Blind antibiotics before cultures compromise every subsequent result.
Reassessment after several hours is part of the investigation, not an optional extra.
explanation.pearls: Occult bacteraemia rates in febrile children aged 3 to 36 months fell from around 3 to 5 in 100 before conjugate pneumococcal vaccination to under 1 in 100 afterwards, which is the single fact that reshaped this pathway.
